lines.para: From 1881, pogroms drive hundreds of thousands of Jews out of the Russian Empire. Between 120,000 and 150,000 settle in Britain, most of them in London’s East End. Whitechapel becomes a shtetl of blackened brick: sweatshops, overcrowded lodging houses, Yiddish in every street.

Children grow up outdoors. Some sell newspapers, others pick pockets. The leaders of the long-established Jewish community worry: every young Jewish delinquent feeds the anti-immigrant press. They fund schools, charities and a reform school where boys learn a trade and discipline.
For the hard cases, there is emigration. Between 1869 and the 1930s, more than 100,000 poor children from Britain are sent to Canada to work on farms.
They are promised air and room to breathe.
